# Course Description

These days, "social networks" are everywhere. Yet, before networking and social media became buzzwords (e.g., before you were born), they were (and continue to be) a field of rigorous study in the social sciences known as **social network analysis** (SNA). In fact, networks became central in sociology during the 1960s and 1970s because they were used to take such fuzzy concepts as "social relationships," "social ties," "groups," "roles," and "social structures" from being evocative abstractions that explained everything (and therefore nothing) to concrete topics of empirical research and social-scientific measurement.

In this course, we will explore this more concrete and "scientific" part of social networks. We will see that the field of study of social networks is distinctive for not only having its own set of theories and concepts (and associated "lingo") but also for the way in which these concepts are immediately made tangible in mathematical (usually quantitative) form using the tools of graph theory and matrix algebra. In Social Network Analysis (SNA), there is thus no clear separation between the theory and the analysis. Another distinctive feature of SNA compared to other areas of sociology is that it is not thematically restricted. Instead, SNA comprises a general set of analytic tools for studying social processes in _any_ field of sociology. This course will thus reflect that thematic diversity.

# Thematic Sequence

The course is designed to introduce you to the entire panoply of concepts and theories that form the core of the field of SNA, as well as the relevant measurement and mathematical representation tools. This field has a long history, but today it is a massive project that recruits people from across the social sciences. Because the primary tools of SNA are graph theory and matrix algebra, throughout the quarter we will jump back and forth between conceptual discussion and mathematical representation, interspersing the more "math-heavy" parts of the class with the more "concept-heavy" parts focusing on social network theory.

Beginning in week 4, we will switch over to substantive theories about how social networks work, focusing on the case of status attainment. The second half of the class will broaden the scope as we explore how various social phenomena—from collaboration and creativity, to status, hierarchy, negative interactions, the diffusion of innovations (and disease), and "the small world"—can be understood from a social network perspective.

# Learning Goals and Objectives

By the end of the course, you should be able to:

*   Understand basic network concepts and theories.
*   Use social-scientific terminology to describe patterns of structure and change observed in networks.
*   Understand and be capable of using measures based on graph theory and matrix algebra to analyze and describe social networks.
*   Understand how social network concepts, theory, and measures can be applied to shed light on a wide variety of phenomena across different fields of study in the social sciences and beyond.

# Organization of the Class

_This is how each week of the class is organized:_

*   **Meeting Times:** The official lecture meeting times for this class are **Tuesdays and Thursdays (TR), 11:00 am -- 12:15 pm** in **Royce Hall Room 362**. In addition, you will attend your assigned TA-led discussion section. Attendance and active engagement at TA-led section meetings are required, as this is where your participation grades will be coming from.

*   **Lectures:** Attendance at the lecture is not required, but it is **strongly** encouraged. In fact, _the best predictor of doing well in the class is regular attendance at the lecture_. Asking questions and taking notes during live delivery of the material aids learning and retention.

*   **Lecture Slides:** All slides on which lectures are based can be found on the associated lesson page on Bruin Learn. Note that these are live slides (their contents are bound to change).

*   **Course Textbook & Readings:** There are no physical textbooks required for purchase. All required readings come from the free online textbook and lesson materials on Bruin Learn:
    *   [SOC 111 Online Textbook: Social Networks](https://olizardo.github.io/networks-textbook/)

*   **Preparation:** To prepare for each class, read the assigned material in advance, including slides and textbook readings, take notes, and prepare questions about concepts that remain unclear.

# Course Requirements

*   **Homework Exercises (60% of the final grade / 135 points)**: Starting in Week 2, there will be **9 weekly homework assignments** (15 points each) designed to help you understand and apply the theories, concepts, and techniques that we will be learning in class. Homework assignments are **due on Mondays by 11:59 pm PT** via Bruin Learn. Instructions and submission links for each homework are available on Bruin Learn.

*   **Biweekly Quizzes (30% of the final grade / 90 points)**: This class has **no final or midterm exams**. Instead, you will take five (5) quizzes **every two weeks** covering the lecture material from the previous two weeks. These are **timed quizzes** (20 minutes) consisting of 18 multiple-choice questions designed to evaluate your understanding and capacity to apply theories, concepts, and definitions. Quizzes open on Friday mornings at 8:00 am and are **due on Sunday nights by 11:59 pm PT** via Bruin Learn. If you have CAE accommodations, they will be applied automatically.

*   **Section Engagement (10% of the final grade / 30 points)**: Because this is a large lecture class, attendance and participation at TA-led discussion sections will be your primary form of graded participation. Section meetings are planned to be in-person only. You get one discussion section absence as a freebie. After that, each unexcused absence results in a penalty on your section engagement grade.

# Expectations and Policies

## Participation

You are expected to participate in section meetings. If you are unsure of how best to participate, talk to the instructor or your TA.

## Homework Assignments

*   **Do the homework:** Homework builds your network muscles! Work in groups (up to 5 people) if you wish, but each student must submit their own solution in their own words.
*   **Due Days & Times:** All homework assignments are **due on Mondays by 11:59 pm PT**.
*   **Do Not Copy Solutions:** Copied solutions will be reported to the Dean of Students for Academic Misconduct.
*   **Late Policy:** Late homework loses 3 points out of 15 (20%) for each day late. In accordance with the 5-day late policy, homework will not be accepted more than 5 days after the due date (locking on Saturdays at 11:59 pm PT).

## Quizzes

Quizzes consist of 18 multiple-choice questions. They are open-book, timed tests administered via Bruin Learn (not in person) lasting 20 minutes. Quizzes are administered on scheduled biweekly dates, **opening on Friday at 8:00 am PT and due on Sunday nights by 11:59 pm PT**. Make-ups are granted only for documented medical or family emergencies.

# Frequently Asked Questions

*   _I don't like the time my discussion section meets. Can I join another one?_

> **No.** You are assigned to the discussion section by the registrar and section sizes must remain balanced. You may only switch if you arrange a direct swap with another student and notify both TAs.

*   _Is there a discussion in the first week?_

> **No.** There are no discussion section meetings during Week 0. Discussions begin in Week 1.

*   _Do we need to do the readings before or after the lecture?_

> **Yes.** Lectures make far more sense if you read before lecture and review afterward.

*   _There are a bunch of formulas! Do I have to memorize each and every one?_

> **No.** Only a few basic formulas (clearly indicated in lecture) will be consulted for quiz questions.

*   _There are many concepts and terms. Do I need to know every definition?_

> **No.** The lecture slides are your guide to what is tested. If a term is in both the lecture and textbook, it will likely be on a quiz.

*   _When should I turn my homework in?_

Check Bruin Learn for each assignment's specific deadline.

*   _I fell behind, and now I want some extra credit. Can I please get some?_

> **No.** The course is structured so that keeping up with regular assignments ensures you do well.

*   _I am on the waiting list. Can you let me in?_

> **No.** Section sizes cannot exceed room/enrollment capacity. You must wait for an open spot via the registrar.
